content:
See PR #42008

I need uniform integrability for ENNReal-valued functions, which is not covered by the current file MeasureTheory.Function.UniformIntegrable.

There are currently two solutions:

  1. The initial PR: Write a separate file for ENNReal-valued functions (see the file UniformIntegrable.lean in the linked PR). Afterwards, rewrite the file for Lp functions to use the lemmas developped for ENNReal-valued functions.
  2. @Yongxi Lin (Aaron) suggestion: extend where possible the current file to cover ENNReals, by replacing NormedAddCommGroup instances with ESeminormedAddMonoid instances.

Both require quite some work, so I'd like to have a consensus about the solution and some implementation details before starting.

Advantages of option 1:

  • Lemmas are immediately usable when dealing with ENNReal-valued functions, without needing a simplification step (set p=1, simplify...)
  • When writing the Lp norm version, decouples what concerns the enorm and what concerns the integrals, which should break down and simplify proofs.
  • Probably more flexible if one needs variants which don't quite fit into the setting of Lp norms.

Advantages of option 2:

  • Generalizes the Lp-version of uniform integrability, including Lp-versions of ENNReal-valued functions which are not covered by the current PR.
  • Avoids duplication and provides a single framework for uniform integrability.

A major obstacle with the second option is that the current file is extremely messy, and replacing NormedAddCommGroup with ESeminormedAddMonoidis far from trivial (the option 1 has the advantage of basically starting from scratch on the Lp version). To give an example, lemma MeasureTheory.MemLp.eLpNorm_indicator_le is at the end of a 200-lines proof, which uses many times Lp spaces, with some intermediates lemmas which are not even expressible in a ESeminormedAddMonoid setting. Hence we are looking at least at a complete rewrite of large parts of the file.

If we go with Option 2, I also think it would be nice to go further and use the current PR as a guide about what is doable in terms of clarity and optimality of hypotheses. For instance, the definition of UnifIntegrable could be replaced by

Tendsto (fun ε ↦ ⨆ (i : ι) (s : Set α) (_ : μ s ≤ ε), eLpNorm (s.indicator (f i)) p μ) (𝓝 0) (𝓝 0)

(less coercions -- ε is an ENNReal instead of a real --, use of filters and sup instead of a long chain of quantifiers, and the measurability hypothesis may not be needed); the notion of UniformTail is pretty useful, and the PR is also, I think, optimal in terms of measurability hypotheses, which could simplify/extend some lemmas.

Any input is welcome, whether it is about the choice between the two options or their implementation.

I feel very strongly that route 2 is the better way to go, even if it is more work to do it.

We had the same issue with L^p-functions and related concepts in the Carleson project, because we wanted to say that functions with ENNReal codomain are L^p. @Michael Rothgang put in a herculean effort to generalize many basic measure-theoretic notions to classes that have an enorm (such as ESeminormedAddMonoid). A lot more of measure theory could be done using these classes, but we haven't pushed it further, since we don't have an immediate need for it.

So route 2 probably requires a bunch of PRs generalizing already existing Mathlib lemmas from the normed world to the enormed world, but I think that is an improvement already.

I don't know much about uniform integrability, so I will not comment much on the definition change. But the new definition looks slick. (Somewhat related: @Felix Pernegger is working on changing the definition of eLpNorm so that it is ∞\infty∞ when the function is not strongly measurable, though he is currently focusing on some more urgent things.)

To explain why I feel strongly about it: if we split the notion, then everything that uses this notion (and works for functions in a generic codomain) has to be duplicated. At the moment this is maybe not that much, but it will only grow over time.
I strongly agree with Floris. Part of mathlib's mission is "find the right abstraction" (even if that means taking a little longer to develop), and enorms seem like a clear step forward.

Damien Thomine said:

A major obstacle with the second option is that the current file is extremely messy

That would be nice to fix, too! :grinning:

Damien Thomine said:

To give an example, lemma MeasureTheory.MemLp.eLpNorm_indicator_le is at the end of a 200-lines proof, which uses many times Lp spaces, with some intermediates lemmas which are not even expressible in a ESeminormedAddMonoid setting.

Does it uses bundled Lp-spaces, i.e. docs#MeasureTheory.Lp ? That would indeed be annoying to translate directly. Does the proof need any nontrivial results from linear algebra / functional analysis about L^p-spaces? If not, it is in my experience easier to work with plain functions and the MemLp predicate.
I cannot promise I'll have a lot of time, but in principle I'm happy to help with norm enorm generalizations.
And indeed, cleaning up the current file (also in terms of statements, generality of hypotheses etc.) will be an excellent first step.

Damien Thomine said:

ε is an ENNReal instead of a real

I agree on we should change the type of ε in the current definition of UnifIntegrable. The case that ε = ∞ is a trivial condition and changing the type allows us to get rid of ENNReal.ofReal in the definition (similarly for the type of δ).

Let me also mention that the equivalent definition of UniformIntegrable that uses Tendsto also appears in @Francesco N. Chotuck's PR #40788 (although the formulation is a bit different there).

If we are going to redefine UnifIntegrable via Tendsto, I think a cleaner formulation, equivalent to Damien's proposal, is:

def UnifIntegrable {α β ι : Type*} {_ : MeasurableSpace α} [ENorm β] [Zero β]
    (f : ι → α → β) (p : ℝ≥0∞) (μ : Measure α) : Prop :=
  Tendsto (fun s ↦ ⨆ i, eLpNorm (s.indicator (f i)) p μ) (comap μ (𝓝 0)) (𝓝 0)

Floris van Doorn said:

eLpNorm so that it is ∞\infty∞ when the function is not strongly measurable

doesn't it mean that the Tendsto version does not work without assuming Measurable s? (you could get non-measurable sets of arbitrarily small outer measure, and the eLpNorm would not be close to 0)
(and I'm curious, why do you need this for the Kac's lemma? but possibly off-topic)

Lua Viana Reis said:

doesn't it mean that the Tendsto version does not work without assuming Measurable s? (you could get non-measurable sets of arbitrarily small outer measure, and the eLpNorm would not be close to 0)

The Tendsto-formulation should use eLpNorm f p (μ.restrict s) instead of Set.indicator. If we do that, then we don't need measurability of s.
We don't need measurability either way, the reduction to the measurable case is not that hard.
It will be hard (and false) after we redefine eLpNorm to be ∞\infty∞ when the function is not measurable, if you use Set.indicator.
Thanks for the information! I'll do that.

I've written PR#42092 as the first step towards this goal. It removes coercions in the definition of UnifIntegrable and changes the definition to a Tendsto version (I like Francesco's suggestion in theory, but wouldn't quite make it work well in practice).

Next steps would be streamlining and changing the proofs throughout the file -- I think I will draw from my non-merged work on LIntegrable versions -- then weakening the hypotheses to ESemiNormedMonoid where possible.

@Lua Viana Reis : For Kac's lemma in ergodic theory, a first step is proving that the first return map of a conservative measure-preserving dynamical system is again measure-preserving. This goes through a "finite-time" formula (valid whenever the return time is at most N), then taking the limit as N->infty.

To prove that the formulas converge to the right limit, I need something like "if f is integrable and T is measure-preserving, then (f o T^n) is uniformly integrable". Due to some specific applications (e.g. Kac's formula), I prefer to work with ENNReal-valued functions f, which are not covered by the current files.
